items.name: p1
items.direction: Narrate this as a high-energy, feel-good fact-list video for BHUGOL, a popular geography fun-facts YouTube channel. The Narrator is thrilled to be telling you this: enthusiastic, upbeat, bright and very expressive, like an excited friend who can't wait to show you something amazing. Big smile in the voice the whole way. Wide, lively pitch movement: rise with real curiosity on every question, hit 'Wrong!' and 'Right?' with playful delight after a tiny comic pause, and say every number with genuine amazement, as if it surprises you too. Announce each 'Fact one!', 'Fact two!' and so on like a bright, punchy game-show call. Land each punchline with a grin. Pace is quick and bouncy, about 170 words per minute, with short crisp pauses; never slow, flat, calm, sleepy or documentary-serious. Accent: native General American English narrator, neutral American accent from the first word to the last. VOICE IDENTITY: always the same warm baritone host, same person and same energy level from the first line to the last. Read numbers naturally. Pronounce Nishinoshima as 'nee-shee-NOH-shee-mah', Aogashima as 'ah-oh-gah-SHEE-mah', Kagoshima as 'kah-GOH-shee-mah', Sakurajima as 'sah-koo-rah-JEE-mah', and Seiryu Miharashi as 'SAY-ryoo mee-hah-RAH-shee'. Pronounce 'Bhoogol' as 'BHOO-gol'.
lines: I bet you a hundred dollars you won't believe these are real. A train station in Japan where, if you get off, you could never walk out. A village on a volcano that has another volcano inside it. A city with ash in its weather forecast. And a summit with no address. Plus two more I'm not telling you yet. But every single one is. And I'll show you the proof. So how does one of the best-mapped countries on Earth keep getting its own map wrong? Grab a red pen. We're fixing the map of Japan. Six times.

Fact one. Rewind to 1987. Japan's coast guard counts its islands. By hand, on paper maps. Total: 6,852. But on paper, two islands close together look like one. An island hugging the shore looks like mainland. So Japan recounts, with digital maps. The new total, in 2023? 14,125. More than double. Zero new land. Japan just looked closer. But Japan does make brand-new land. From nothing.

Fact two. Nishinoshima, about 1,000 kilometres south of Tokyo. In 2013, the sea beside it started steaming, and a new island rose out of the water. Weeks later, it crashed into Nishinoshima. The two became one. The lava kept coming. Today the island is more than ten times its old size. Officially, it's part of Tokyo. So the capital is growing. By volcano. Of course, nobody lives there. Living on a volcano would be ridiculous. Right?

Fact three. Aogashima. Also... Tokyo. The whole island is a volcano. And inside its crater sits a second, smaller one. About 160 people live here. Japan's smallest village. In 1785, an eruption emptied the island for about 50 years. Then people came back. On purpose. Today the volcano heats the village sauna and steams their eggs. Our next volcano isn't so calm.

lines: Fact four. Kagoshima, a city of about 600,000. Right across the bay sits Sakurajima, the most active volcano in Japan. In 2011, it erupted more than 1,000 times. Over three a day. So here, the weather report also tells you where the ash will fall. People check it before doing laundry. Forecast for today: sunny, with a chance of volcano. So surely Japan's most famous volcano belongs to Japan? Well... not the top.

Fact five. Mount Fuji. Above the 8th station, the summit isn't government land. It belongs to a shrine. The state took it once. The shrine sued to get it back, and won. And here's the twist. Two prefectures share Fuji, and they've never drawn the border across the top. So Japan's mapping agency took the summit's address off its online map. Japan's highest point. Address: unknown. But at least you can leave Mount Fuji. Our last stop, you can't.

Fact six. A quiet valley in western Japan. In 2019, a railway opens a station here, above a river. It has a platform. A sign. A view. What it doesn't have is a road. Or a path. Or an exit. Even its building materials came in by train, at night. It's called Seiryu Miharashi, "clear stream viewpoint." Only special trains stop. You step off, look at the river, and wait for the train back.

So, our map. Uncounted islands. Growing land. A volcano in a volcano. Ash forecasts. A summit with no address. A station with no exit. Japan's map was never really wrong. Japan just won't sit still. Which leaves you on that platform, with plenty of time to count islands. So, how many did you believe? Be honest. Because
